title: How to Improve Teaching (Version 2)
author: South Glous Head
summary: Writing anonymously as "South Glous Head," a headteacher with 17 years of school-improvement experience lays out five best bets for improving teaching quality, explicitly declining to make grand pedagogical proclamations in favour of practical leadership lessons learned the hard way. Their first principle is diagnostic patience: too much school improvement jumps straight to a trendy or borrowed solution without first forensically understanding the actual problem, a mistake they admit took their own school nearly four years to correct around reading instruction. Their second principle, drawing on Jim Collins, argues real commitment to a strategy requires abandoning the one-off INSET-day model in favour of five or more spaced training sessions that keep returning to and refining the same practice. They also describe giving middle leaders substantial non-contact thinking and research time, and building staff book groups around a single shared improvement focus (this year, retrieval practice) to give teachers genuine agency in shaping the schoolwide approach rather than just receiving it top-down. The piece culminates in an account of accidentally landing on a singular pedagogy - one shared slide-deck template for lesson structure used across all subjects, including PE and art - which staff embraced once they'd helped build it, and which the author credits with reducing teachers' cognitive load by cutting the number of distinct approaches they need to remember from dozens down to roughly five.
points: The headteacher's first best bet is diagnostic discipline: resisting the pull toward whatever's trending on Edutwitter or copying a halo school down the road without first forensically identifying the actual problem, which took four years to get right themselves.

Their second principle borrows Jim Collins's "if you have more than three priorities, you don't have any" to argue against one-off INSET training days, insisting new practices need five or more spaced-out training sessions to actually stick.

The singular pedagogy approach - one shared slide-deck template for lesson structure across all subjects - emerged partly by accident but is credited with reducing teacher cognitive load by cutting distinct pedagogical approaches from dozens to roughly five.

The piece explicitly frames standardisation as compatible with teacher autonomy, arguing staff embrace agreed approaches more readily when they've helped design and refine them through structured book groups and research time.
quotes: Improving teaching is one of the main jobs of a Headteacher – the clue is in the title.

Indeed, for disadvantaged children, the quality of the teacher in front of them every day has more impact on their learning than any number of interventions, tutoring programs, swanky resources or even the quality of the building.
Too much school improvement planning lacks both detailed analysis of the problem, and a clear exploration of all the potential solutions, before diving into a chosen approach.
Jim Collins once wisely proclaimed that ‘if you have more than three priorities, then you don’t have any priorities’. This is almost certainly the case with most School Development Planning.
So, to make something stick, it needs to be constantly returned to over weeks and months. One review staff meeting following the INSET simply won’t cut it.
This therefore levels the playing field between a teacher who has twenty years of experience and one who has two years. It takes the guesswork out of teaching.
We had received some excellent training from Adam Robins, who made this exact point – teachers have too much to remember, so give them less!
